Everyone welcome Masala, Saffron’s miracle baby, to the Chattanooga Zoo!
 Masala was born earlier in July when one of the zoo’s keepers Dominique Daniel noticed signs of Saffron going into labor — even though her pregnancy wasn’t confirmed. While the zoo suspected Saffron to be pregnant, a reproductive process called delayed implantation affected the timeline and made it difficult to fully confirm.
 We’re so happy about this good news for Saffron, especially after her mate Avi passed earlier this year! Celebrate the birth of Masala with a gender reveal party on October 18 from 1:30-4:30.

items.content_text:
Exploring Downtown: The Maclellan House 
 Tucked into the Bluff View Art District, the Maclellan House holds more than a century of Chattanooga history within its walls.
 Built in the late 1800s, the house was home to just two families: the Maclellans and, later, the Bryans. Many of the families’ original heirloom furnishings remain inside today, giving visitors a glimpse of what the home looked and felt like generations ago. 
 The house also has connections to Chattanooga’s broader history. Thomas Maclellan founded Provident Life & Accident Insurance Company, which later became part of Unum. His descendants later established the Maclellan Foundation, which continues its philanthropic work in Chattanooga today. 
 Today, the Maclellan House has been restored as a seven-room bed and breakfast. It was the oldest and last of Bluff View’s three historic inn homes to be restored, with much of the character and detail of the original residence still intact.
 More than a century after it was built, the Maclellan House offers a chance to step inside a piece of Chattanooga history that has been carefully preserved.

The International Bluegrass Music Association's World of Bluegrass is taking over Chattanooga October 20-24, filling our city with bluegrass through a multi-day conference, evening concerts across multiple venues, a weekend music festival, and an all-day community event: Pickin' in the Park. 
 Pickin' in the Park is a free, outdoor festival happening in the heart of downtown. It celebrates music, local artists, and our community. 
 Mark your calendars. Grab your lawn chairs and blankets. We hope to see you there!
Everything you need to know about Pickin’ in the Park 👉
 Y’all come on down to Miller Park and Miller Plaza on Saturday, October 24 for a full day of live music featuring college bands, Kids on Bluegrass bands, and local Chattanooga talent. 🎶
 And don’t miss a special live performance from @randysteele and the Chattanooga Ballet! 🩰
 Plus, grab some food from local food trucks and shop arts & crafts vendors throughout the day.
 🌳 Open air
 🎟️ No tickets required
 🚧 No fencing
 If you come to Pickin’ in the Park and find yourself needing even more bluegrass in your life, consider grabbing a ticket to IBMA Bluegrass Live!®, the ticketed portion of the event. Single- and two-day tickets are on sale now at worldofbluegrass.org.
 Pickin’ in the Park is presented by the City of Chattanooga and Hamilton County. Special thanks to Chattanooga Tourism Co. and River City Company.
 Learn more about the College Band Showcase at https://bluegrassfoundation.org/higher-ed-resources/.
 #IBMA #VisitChatt #chattanoogaballet #chattanoogamusic #bluegrassfestival Visit Chattanooga

Commission Meeting Summary – October 5, 2026 
 Southern Adventist University MOU (Resolution 585): The commission approved a Memorandum of Understanding with Southern Adventist University. The city's partnership with SAU's School of Nursing began in 2025 with Storm Safety Day, and this MOU continues it. The agreement is needed mainly to cover liability for the event. 
 Airport Advisory Board Liaison (Resolution 586): The commission approved a motion to amend the resolution so the liaison's term ends in 2028 instead of 2027 and to appoint Vice Mayor Sadler as the commission's liaison to the Airport Advisory Board. 
 City Administration Report – 
 - Near Cambridge Square Development: Conversations are ongoing about a proposed development across from Cambridge Square. 
 - Railroad Crossing Cameras: Iron Rail Cams is reviewing the MOU for its crossing camera. 
 - Parks & Rec Board: The city is revising the Parks & Recreation Board ordinances. 
 - Library Ordinance: A library ordinance has been drafted as the city will take over library operations January 1, 2027. 
 - Free Community Shred Event: The event is next Tuesday, October 13th from 3 to 6 PM in the City Hall parking lot. 
 Commissioner Reports – 
 - Flock Cameras: Residents have been calling to ask whether the Flock cameras are still recording, and Commissioner Johnson deferred to the police chief. The chief confirmed the cameras are disconnected and no one has access to them. Flock has also acknowledged the city's notice of termination. To reassure residents, the commission has decided to cover the cameras with black trash bags, using Public Works' bucket truck until the cameras are removed by Flock. 
 - Rockslide Cleanup: Commissioner Johnson thanked Public Works for quickly clearing the large rocks that slid down the bank off Innovation Drive. Because the rocks damaged a fence, staff are meeting with a fence contractor about repairs. 
 - National Night Out: Commissioner Howse said she is looking forward to National Night Out. 
 Watch the full meeting: https://play.champds.com/collegedaletn/event/160

🚀 The future of technology is happening right here in Chattanooga!
 And the City of Red Bank got a firsthand look. 👀💻
 This past Friday, Stormwater Supervisor Louis Brill, IT Director Stacey Bradley, and Solid Waste Supervisor Scott Johnson, had the opportunity to tour EPB’s new Quantum Center — America’s first commercial quantum computing and networking hub!
 🤯 So… what exactly is quantum technology?
 While it may sound like something straight out of a sci-fi movie, this emerging technology could one day help communities tackle some pretty big challenges — from infrastructure planning and transportation to utility management, cybersecurity, and more.
 At Red Bank, we believe staying ahead means staying curious. We’re always looking for opportunities to learn about new technology, connect with regional leaders, and explore tools that could help us provide better, more efficient services to our residents.
 A big thank you to EPB for giving our team a behind-the-scenes look at this exciting new technology! We’re excited to see what the future holds for Chattanooga and the entire region. 🌐⚡
 Who knows? The technology of tomorrow might already be right in our backyard. 👏
 #EPBQuantum #Innovation #FutureReady #RedBankTN #Chattanooga

items.content_text:
"Young people don't just want to be taught how to recycle, but rather they want ecosystems of engagement that combine personal action with structural power."

That was the message from our young peer research team to over 100 policymakers, politicians and practitioners from across youth and climate sectors at London's City Hall.

For the past two years, we've been mapping how London's green transition is being shaped by young people, and what could strengthen their voices. At the end of last month, the peer researchers shared findings from interviews across 18 London boroughs, kicking off a World Café guided by nine guest speakers.

We shared innovative tools and methods - from youth-led social action projects to policy co-design to political storytelling. We had frank conversations about the limits of current efforts, and about examples that inspired our research team. Together, we workshopped strategies for embedding youth participation in local administrations, and for building "ecosystems of engagement" that put young people at the centre of shaping a greener and more just future for their city.

Thank you to everyone who attended, to Partnership for Young London and Islington Council for co-delivering this project with LSE Cities, to the Greater London Authority for hosting us, and above all to the peer research team for making it all possible: Phool Ashraf, Cindy Boa; Jakaria Uddin; Maddy Westhead. 

Thanks also to our speakers: Cllr Rowena Champion, Isabella Tanner, Samia Dumbuya, Tim Alcroft, Pip Sayers, Stephanie F., Carlos Izsak, Martha Dillon, Bronwyn Hayward MNZM she/her, to Zoë Wilkins from the GLA, and to project coordinators Imogen Hamilton-Jones, Matthew Walsham, and Monika Milewska.

items.content_text:
**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**
 October 5, 2026
 Hamilton County Health & Social Services, Erlanger Hospital, and Community Partners Unite to Encourage Vaccinations Ahead of Cold and Flu Season
 HAMILTON COUNTY, TN— Hamilton County Health & Social Services, Erlanger Hospital, and community partners are joining forces to encourage residents to protect themselves, their families, and the broader community by staying current on recommended and school-required vaccinations ahead of cold and flu season.
 Local health and medical leaders are reminding residents about the importance of vaccination and the community resources available to help families access potentially lifesaving vaccines.
 Respiratory illnesses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) circulate more widely during the fall and winter. Vaccination remains an important tool for reducing the risk of serious illness and protecting vulnerable community members. RSV can cause serious respiratory illness, particularly among infants, young children, and older adults.
 “In the pediatric ICU, we care for children who may have been healthy a week ago and now need help breathing. RSV and the flu can both have that effect on a baby or young child, and very quickly. Some may need oxygen, some may need a breathing tube, and some spend days in intensive care,” said Dr. Marvin Hall, Chief Medical Officer for the Children’s Hospital at Erlanger. “The Children's Hospital at Erlanger sees this each winter. We're coming together as a community now because the best time to protect a child is before these viruses start spreading. An RSV immunization and a flu shot this fall can keep many families out of the hospital.”
 Health officials also encourage parents and caregivers to review their children’s vaccination records and confirm that they are current on all school-required vaccines. Keeping children up to date helps protect individual students and reduce the spread of vaccine-preventable illnesses in schools, daycares, and the broader community.
 As part of this community-wide effort, the Hamilton County Health Department will participate in the statewide Fight Flu TN initiative by offering free flu shots to individuals ages six months and older on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.
 “Each year, we see firsthand how detrimental flu season can be to our community. It can mean missed days of school or work, increased visits to healthcare providers, and for some, serious illness & hospitalization,” said Dr. Stephen Miller, Health Officer for Hamilton County. “That is why Fight Flu TN is so vital. We must ensure everyone in our community has low-barrier access to potentially lifesaving vaccines. By making the flu shot free and easily accessible, we are giving more people the opportunity to protect themselves and our community.”
 Free flu shots will be available at: 
 Location – Adults and Children:
 • J.A. Henry Community YMCA:
 o 9:00 a.m. – 1:00 p.m.
 o 3500 Dodds Ave #108, Chattanooga, TN 37407
 • The Samaritan Center (The Health Department’s Mobile Unit)
 o 9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.
 o 9231 Lee Hwy, Ooltewah, TN 37363
 Details:
 • No appointment or insurance is required.
 • Adults 18+ and children ages six months and older may participate.
 • Children’s vaccines are available at all flu vaccination event sites.
 • ONLY FREE THIS DAY – while supplies last.
 • Bilingual staff & an ASL interpreter will be on site(s).
 The flu vaccine is safe and effective. It can protect against common types of influenza and reduce the risk of the virus’s most serious symptoms and outcomes. Nationally, flu vaccination is estimated to have prevented approximately 10 million illnesses, 5 million medical visits, 180,000 hospitalizations, and 12,000 deaths during the 2024–2025 influenza season.
 Pregnant people, infants, older adults, and individuals with chronic medical conditions face a higher risk of severe flu complications. Flu symptoms may include coughing, fatigue, fever, headache, muscle aches, sore throat, and a stuffy or runny nose.
 For more information about precautions against respiratory viral illnesses, including influenza, visit the Tennessee Department of Health’s Respiratory Viral Illness webpage.
 Additional resources 
 • Questions? Call the Health Department at 423-209-8000.
 • Free interpretation services are available at all Health Department clinics. 
 • For Health Department information, visit: Health.HamiltonTN.org
 • To read this information in Spanish, visit the Health Department’s Spanish Facebook page at https://www.facebook.com/SaludHamiltonTN

items.title: Informal work – which isn't covered by national labour laws, is not taxed and does not provide pension rights
items.content_text:
Informal work – which isn't covered by national labour laws, is not taxed and does not provide pension rights – is the norm for billions of workers. In some countries, economic growth has even coincided with rising informal employment.
 Across countries covered by a new #OECD report, 68% of workers are employed informally, with 16% of those informal workers being in highly paid jobs and possibly choosing to remain informal.
 Securing the Livelihoods of Informal Economy Workers in Times of Global Changes, launched today, provides insights on the diversity of informal work and how population ageing, the automation of work and environmental risks are reshaping the livelihoods of informal workers.
 Key findings:
 ➡️ Informal workers earn 44% less per hour than formal workers, limiting their ability to build financial security and withstand economic shocks.
 ➡️ One in three informal workers holds a job at high risk of being automated, nearly twice the rate among formal workers.
 ➡️ Informal workers are especially vulnerable to environmental degradation, particularly in developing countries where many depend on the natural environment for their livelihoods. More than 40% of informal workers face medium to high risks from floods and droughts, compared to less than 2% of formal workers.

Informal work – which isn't covered by national labour laws, is not taxed and does not provide pension rights – is the norm for billions of workers. In some countries, economic growth has even coincided with rising informal employment.
Across countries covered by a new #OECD report, 68% of workers are employed informally, with 16% of those informal workers being in highly paid jobs and possibly choosing to remain informal.
Securing the Livelihoods of Informal Economy Workers in Times of Global Changes, launched today, provides insights on the diversity of informal work and how population ageing, the automation of work and environmental risks are reshaping the livelihoods of informal workers.
Key findings:
➡️ Informal workers earn 44% less per hour than formal workers, limiting their ability to build financial security and withstand economic shocks.
➡️ One in three informal workers holds a job at high risk of being automated, nearly twice the rate among formal workers.
➡️ Informal workers are especially vulnerable to environmental degradation, particularly in developing countries where many depend on the natural environment for their livelihoods. More than 40% of informal workers face medium to high risks from floods and droughts, compared to less than 2% of formal workers.
As demographic shifts, technological change and environmental pressures increase risks to the livelihoods of informal workers, effective policies to strengthen their resilience are crucial for sustainable and inclusive economic growth.

items.content_text:
We are delighted to share that LSE Cities researchers have been recognised in two categories at the 2026 LSE Impact Prize, celebrating excellent engagement, impact and culture across the School. 🏆 

Dr Philipp Rode, Charlie Hicks and Dr Alexandra Gomes received the Outstanding team impact prize for their work on fair car use budgeting and urban transport policy. 

The team developed UrbanMiles, a digital tool that uses road-space data to estimate how far people can travel by car before causing gridlock. The research helps policymakers and the public explore questions of fairness in how limited urban road space is allocated. Working with partners, the team also contributed to deliberative processes that informed Hackney Council’s transport strategy. 

Dr Alexandra Gomes, alongside Dr Asseel Al-Ragam, Sharifa Alshalfan, Tanushree Agarwal and Joao Peres, was also named a runner-up in the Outstanding engagement category for Kuwaitscapes, developed in partnership with LSE Middle East Centre which uses a card game and digital participation platform to make urban research more accessible and encourage civic engagement around public space and sustainable urban living. 

Congratulations to all our colleagues and collaborators on this recognition.

🔗 Find out more about all the LSE Impact Prize winners: https://lnkd.in/eiJWH9hx

#LSEImpactPrize #UrbanResearch #UrbanPolicy #TransportPolicy #CivicEngagement #Cities

💙 Today is Bullying Prevention Day!

Creating a safe and supportive school community is something we all have a role in. Whether you are a student, staff member, family member or community member, small actions can make a big difference.

What can you do?

▪️ Speak up. If you see someone being bullied, safely step in or get a trusted adult to help.

▪️ Be there. Listen to and support someone who may be experiencing bullying. Sometimes, simply knowing someone cares can make a big difference.

▪️ Learn more. Understanding what bullying looks like and how it can affect someone helps us recognize it and respond.

▪️ Choose kindness. Look for ways to include others, encourage your classmates and create a welcoming environment.

Together, we can help make Hamilton County Schools a place where every student feels safe, valued and like they belong.

items.content_text:
Growing up in poverty or socio-economic disadvantage can shape a child’s life. Children are more likely to experience poorer health, lower educational achievement and fewer employment opportunities throughout life.  
 Our new report, Spending Better for Children through Social Policy looks at how governments can use social spending to improve children’s lives.  
 Spending more can help, but changing the way we spend can achieve much more.
 The findings show that while additional investment can improve outcomes,  greatest benefits for children are achieved when resources are directed towards a balanced mix of policy packages that combine employment support, adequate income protection and accessible, high-quality public services.
 Getting the policy mix right can improve outcomes for children today. And they prevent costs from showing up later in our economies, including lower productivity, weaker growth and higher public spending. 
 Discover more insights: https://brnw.ch/21x6asW

items.title: Bilateral official development assistance (ODA) for health is projected to fall to its lowest level in almost two decade...
items.content_text:
Bilateral official development assistance (ODA) for health is projected to fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
 ODA is financial support from governments promoting the economic development and welfare of developing countries.
 #OECD projections show that bilateral ODA for health could decline by 29-46% between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to a reduction of USD 5-8 billion. This would bring support back to levels not seen since 2008.
 The decline follows the sharp increase in health ODA during the COVID-19 pandemic. By 2026, funding is projected to be 63% below its 2022 peak, with further reductions expected beyond 2026 as major providers continue to implement multi-year cuts.
 Health was the third-largest sector for bilateral ODA in 2024, receiving USD 17.6 billion, after humanitarian aid and support to government and civil society. The scale of the projected reductions could therefore have significant implications for countries that rely on external financing to support their health systems. 
 Explore the latest data on ODA for health ➡️ https://brnw.ch/21x69RB 
 #ODA2026 #OECDdevelopment

items.content_text:
The Chattanooga Fire Department is teaming up with the National Fire Protection Association to support Fire Prevention Week 2026. This year’s FPW theme, “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” focuses on the simple steps people can take to recharge safely. Safe charging means making smart choices every time you plug in.
 Many devices used in our daily lives - phones, tablets, laptops, tools, toys, e-bikes, and scooters—run on rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which store a lot of energy in a small space. If they are damaged or charged the wrong way, they can overheat, start a fire, or even explode.
 • Use the cord and charger that came with your device or one approved by the manufacturer. Using the wrong charger can damage the battery and increase the risk of fire.
 • Charge devices on a table, desk, or other hard, flat surface. Do not charge them on beds, couches, or under pillows. Devices and chargers produce heat during normal charging. Soft surfaces can trap heat and block airflow, which can cause the battery to overheat.
 • Stop using your device if it feels very hot, starts to swell, is smoking, or has a strange smell. These are warning signs that the battery may be damaged or failing.
 • Unplug your device when it is fully charged. Do not leave it plugged in longer than needed. Leaving a device plugged in too long can increase heat and stress on the battery.
 • Charge larger items like e-bikes, scooters, and power tools outside and away from exits. These batteries are larger and store more energy. If they fail, fires can grow quickly and spread. 
 • When on a plane, keep your device where you can see it while charging. Do not charge devices in overhead compartments. Do not charge e-cigarettes or vapes on a plane. If a battery overheats or fails, it is important for the flight crew to respond quickly.

 Upon arrival crews found flames and smoke visible from the roof of the business. Command established water supply and aerial flow on the roof, while crews initiated interior attack on the main floor. The fire was quickly extinguished.
 No one was inside the business at the time of the incident.
 There were no injuries to CFD personnel.
 The cause is under investigation.

items.content_text:
Today, we celebrated a century of tradition, recreation and community at Brainerd Golf Course, and we couldn’t have asked for a better group to celebrate with, even with a little rain!
 Opened on October 3, 1926, Brainerd was designed by legendary golf architect Donald Ross and created with a simple vision: to provide quality, accessible outdoor recreation for the Chattanooga community.
 One hundred years later, that mission continues. Generations of golfers have made memories on these fairways, and Brainerd remains an important part of Chattanooga’s public golf tradition.
 Special shout out to Greta Hayes-Director of Recreation, Eddie Taylor-Director of Golf, Joe Starr-Director of Maintenance and Edwin Prichard-Brainerd Golf Manager. Combined, these individuals have over 115 years of service with City of Chattanooga golf. 
 Also thank you Mayor Kelly and District 5 Councilman Dennis Clark for sharing a few words. 
 A huge thank you to everyone who came out today, played in the 100 Year Celebration Two-Person Scramble, cheered on the players and helped us celebrate this incredible milestone.
 Here’s to 100 years of Brainerd Golf, and many more to come!

 Among all the uses of artificial intelligence, few have been more divisive than song-demo production.  Wednesday at 4:15

To the ones who replaced steel, sandblasted, replaced the wood plank by plank, protected the Tennessee River below, and so much more — thank you. This bridge is now ready to welcome everyone for the next 136 years!

items.content_text:
In 2024, bilateral donors and EU institutions mobilised USD 23.4 billion in private finance (commercial money channelled towards sustainable development objectives).
 But how was that money mobilised, and where was it invested?
 The 2026 #OECD Development Co-operation Profiles highlight how providers of development assistance are using public resources to attract private investment and which sectors are receiving support.
 Insights include how:
 ➡️ The United States mobilised USD 6.9 billion, followed by EU institutions (USD 6 billion) and Germany (USD 2.5 billion)
 ➡️ The banking and financial services sector accounted for more than one-third of all mobilised private finance
 ➡️ The energy sector represented 23% of the total
 ➡️ Together, banking and financial services and energy attracted more than half of all mobilised private finance in 2024.
 Find out more in the #DCprofiles2026: https://brnw.ch/21x68Gv
 #OECDdevelopment

Every summer, many undergraduate students at the UTC have the opportunity to dive deeper into research and explore new learning experiences. Think about hands-on research, faculty mentorship, lab experience, connecting with peers and exploring new places.
 The National Science Foundation Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) program makes some of these opportunities possible by funding students to spend the summer collaborating on research projects at institutions across the country.
 UTC junior Chloe Mondido is majoring in mechatronics and is a Brock Scholar in the UTC Honors College. The Flintstone, Georgia, native spent 10 weeks participating in an REU program at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, where she worked on developing flexible temperature sensors.
 🔗  Read more here: https://blog.utc.edu/…/research-on-the-road-a-conversation…/
